1.translation: Sañjaya said: To him who sat there overwhelmed by pity, his troubled eyes brimming with tears and his spirit sinking, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
1.nuances: All six agree on the scene; they differ on the compound aśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam, which Sivananda, Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan read as eyes both tear-filled and agitated, while Adidevananda shifts the agitation to a bewildered look and Prabhupada to a depressed mind. Purohit alone recasts the verse as indirect narration and adds that Kṛṣṇa consoled Arjuna.

2.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Where has this faintness come from, Arjuna, at such a critical hour? It is not the way of the noble, it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
2.nuances: The key word kaśmalam is rendered as dejection (Sivananda, Adidevananda), weakness (Purohit), impurity (Gambirananda, Prabhupada) and even sinful act (Sankaranarayan). Anārya is taken socially as Aryans or noble by Purohit, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, but morally as unenlightened by Gambirananda and as a man who knows the value of life by Prabhupada; Prabhupada also turns heaven into higher planets.

3.translation: Do not give in to weakness, Pārtha; it does not suit you. Shake off this petty faintness of heart and stand up, Parantapa.
3.nuances: Klaibyam is unmanliness for Purohit, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, impotence for Sivananda and Prabhupada, with Purohit adding effeminacy. Sankaranarayan oddly renders Pārtha as son of Kuntī, and the translators split between scorcher and chastiser of foes for Parantapa.

4.translation: Arjuna said: How can I turn my arrows against Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle, Madhusūdana? They deserve my reverence, Arisūdana.
4.nuances: Everyone reads the sense the same way; the divergence is in the vocatives, which Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada keep as Madhusūdana and slayer of foes, Adidevananda reduces to slayer of foes alone, and Purohit replaces with My Lord. Pūjārhau ranges from worshipped (Sivananda, Prabhupada) to adoration (Gambirananda) and reverence (Purohit, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan).

5.translation: It would be better to live on alms in this world than to kill these great-souled teachers. If I killed them, every pleasure I enjoyed here, wealth and desire alike, would be smeared with their blood.
5.nuances: The crux is arthakāmān: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Prabhupada attach the wealth and desire to the enjoyments Arjuna would gain, while Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada in his second sentence make it describe the teachers themselves as greedy for wealth. Purohit paraphrases freely, calling the teachers benefactors and omitting the wealth motive.

6.translation: We do not even know which would be better for us, to conquer them or to be conquered by them. The very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra we would not wish to outlive after killing stand before us in the front line.
6.nuances: All agree on the dilemma; the main difference is that Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada keep the plural we, whereas Purohit makes it a personal I. Adidevananda's vanishing is an evident slip for vanquishing.

7.translation: My very nature is crippled by the fault of faint-heartedness and my mind is confused about what is right; I ask you to tell me for certain what is best. I am your disciple; teach me, for I have taken refuge in you.
7.nuances: Kārpaṇya is pity for Sivananda, Purohit and Sankaranarayan, weak commiseration or compassion for Gambirananda and Adidevananda, and miserly weakness for Prabhupada, who alone adds surrendered soul. Purohit reads śreyaḥ explicitly as spiritual welfare and softens the final clause into a prayer.

8.translation: I cannot see what could drive away this grief that is drying up my senses, even if I won an unrivalled and prosperous kingdom on earth, or sovereignty over the gods themselves.
8.nuances: Translators agree on the sense but differ on the image ucchoṣaṇam, rendered burns (Sivananda), paralysing (Purohit), blasting (Gambirananda), withers (Adidevananda), scorcher (Sankaranarayan) and drying up (Prabhupada). Purohit abstracts the kingdoms into visible and invisible worlds and Prabhupada turns the gods into demigods.

9.translation: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, scorcher of foes, told Govinda, "I will not fight," and fell silent.
9.nuances: The translators disagree on whom parantapa addresses: Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada apply it to Arjuna, while Sankaranarayan reads it as Sañjaya's vocative to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Purohit drops the epithets for Lord of All-Hearts and adds O King, and Prabhupada folds Govinda into the quoted speech.

10.translation: Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, almost smiling, spoke these words to him as he sat dejected between the two armies.
10.nuances: Prahasann iva is read very differently: Sivananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada give a plain or gracious smile, Purohit a gracious smile, but Gambirananda renders it as mocking and Adidevananda as smiling by way of ridicule. Purohit omits the vocative Bhārata, which the others take as addressed to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

11.translation: The Blessed Lord said: You grieve for those who need no grieving, and yet you talk like a wise man. The learned grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
11.nuances: Most read prajñāvādān as Arjuna speaking words of wisdom while acting otherwise, but Sankaranarayan inverts it to say he does not talk like a wise man. Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan keep the literal departed and undeparted life, while Prabhupada's title Supreme Personality of Godhead marks his devotional framing.

12.translation: There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men; and none of us will ever cease to exist hereafter.
12.nuances: All six agree on the doctrine of the beginningless and endless self. Gambirananda alone preserves the stacked double negatives of the Sanskrit, while the others smooth them into positive assertions, and janādhipāḥ varies between rulers of men, princes and kings.

13.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on into another body; a steady person is not confused by this.
13.nuances: Dhīra is firm (Sivananda), wise (Purohit, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan), intelligent (Gambirananda) and sober (Prabhupada). Prabhupada explicitly adds at death and continuously, while the rest leave the moment of transition unstated.

14.translation: Contacts with the material world, Kaunteya, bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go and do not last. Endure them, Bhārata.
14.nuances: Mātrāsparśāḥ is read as sense-object contacts by Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, as external relations by Purohit, left untranslated as matras by Sankaranarayan, and expanded by Prabhupada into a seasonal simile about happiness and distress arising from sense perception. Purohit replaces both epithets with O Prince.

15.translation: The person whom these do not disturb, best of men, who is steady and the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.
15.nuances: Amṛtatva is immortality for everyone except Prabhupada, who renders it liberation. Sankaranarayan says such a person becomes immortal rather than being fit for it, and Purohit substitutes hero for the vocative puruṣarṣabha.

16.translation: The unreal has no existence, and the real never ceases to exist; those who see the truth have discerned the final nature of both.
16.nuances: This is the most philosophically loaded verse so far: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda keep the abstract real and unreal, Sankaranarayan glosses it as existence and non-existence, and Prabhupada inserts the material body and the soul in brackets as the referents. Antaḥ is rendered as truth, nature, conclusion or finality.

17.translation: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded; no one can bring about the destruction of that imperishable one.
17.nuances: Sarvam idam is the whole universe for Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, all that we see for Purohit, but only the entire body for Prabhupada, who restricts the pervasion to the individual soul. Purohit and Prabhupada name the referent as Spirit or soul; the others keep the neutral That.

18.translation: These bodies are said to have an end, but the embodied self is eternal, indestructible and beyond measure. Therefore fight, Bhārata.
18.nuances: Aprameya is immeasurable for Sivananda, Purohit and Prabhupada, indeterminable for Gambirananda, and incomprehensible for Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan. Adidevananda labels the self Jiva, Prabhupada living entity, and Purohit substitutes O Valiant Man for Bhārata.

19.translation: Whoever thinks this self is a killer and whoever thinks it is killed, neither understands; it neither kills nor is killed.
19.nuances: All agree on the sense; the difference is the label given to enam, which is Self (Sivananda, Adidevananda), Spirit (Purohit), this One or This (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), and living entity (Prabhupada). Vijānītaḥ is softened to ignorant by Purohit and Adidevananda.

20.translation: It is never born and never dies; having once been, it does not cease to be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.
20.nuances: The clause nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ is read by Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda and Adidevananda as once existing it never ceases, by Sankaranarayan as not having been it will not come to be, and by Prabhupada as a triple denial of coming into being. Prabhupada alone uses the personal pronoun He for the soul.

21.translation: Pārtha, when a person knows this self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and unchanging, how can that person kill anyone, or cause anyone to be killed?
21.nuances: Gambirananda notes the question is a rhetorical denial, and all read it so, but Sankaranarayan uniquely turns ghātayati into a passive be slain. Purohit omits the vocative Pārtha; the others keep it or expand it to son of Pṛthā.

22.translation: Just as a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws off worn-out bodies and takes on others that are new.
22.nuances: All six share the clothing simile without disagreement. The only shading is Sankaranarayan's rightly proceeds for saṃyāti, and Prabhupada's addition of useless to the old bodies.

23.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.
23.nuances: There is no interpretive divergence; the translators differ only in the name they supply for the subject (It, This, the self, the soul) and in verb choice, cut versus cleave, wet versus moisten.

24.translation: It cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried; it is eternal, present everywhere, stable, unmoving and ancient.
24.nuances: Sthāṇu is stable for most, stationary for Gambirananda and unchanging for Purohit and Prabhupada; sanātana is ancient for Sivananda and Purohit but changeless or eternal for Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan. Prabhupada's insoluble and his personal He again mark the individual-soul reading.

25.translation: This self is said to be unmanifest, beyond thought and beyond change. So, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
25.nuances: Avyakta is unmanifest for five translators but invisible for Prabhupada, and Sankaranarayan gives non-evident and imponderable. Prabhupada adds for the body as the object of grief, an interpretive supplement not in the Sanskrit.

26.translation: And even if you think of it as something constantly born and constantly dying, mighty-armed one, even then you should not grieve like this.
26.nuances: All read the concession the same way. Prabhupada alone inserts or the symptoms of life in brackets, and Sankaranarayan makes This the object of lament rather than reading evam as the manner of grieving.

27.translation: For one who is born, death is certain, and for one who dies, birth is certain. So you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
27.nuances: Aparihārye arthe is the inevitable for five translators, but Prabhupada reads it as the unavoidable discharge of your duty, importing the theme of duty. Gambirananda and Adidevananda explicitly gloss the second birth as rebirth.

28.translation: Beings are unmanifest at their beginning, manifest in the middle and unmanifest again at their end, Bhārata. What is there to lament in that?
28.nuances: Avyakta is unmanifest for Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada but unknown for Purohit and Adidevananda, a shift from ontology to epistemology. Prabhupada's annihilated for nidhana is his own emphasis, and Purohit again drops the vocative.

29.translation: One person sees it as a wonder, another speaks of it as a wonder, another hears of it as a wonder; and even after hearing, no one truly knows it.
29.nuances: The last line is read as nobody knows it at all by Sivananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, as scarcely one knows it by Purohit, and as some do not realize it by Gambirananda and Prabhupada, a real difference in how absolute the ignorance is. Prabhupada uses him for the soul throughout.

30.translation: The one who dwells in the body of every being can never be killed, Bhārata. So you should not grieve for any creature.
30.nuances: Purohit departs most sharply, recasting the verse as Be not anxious about these armies and omitting the final injunction. Adidevananda expands dehe sarvasya into a statement about selves in all bodies, while the others keep the single indweller.

31.translation: And considering your own duty too, you should not waver; for a kṣatriya there is nothing better than a battle fought for what is right.
31.nuances: Svadharma is simply duty for most; Prabhupada specifies duty as a kṣatriya and reads dharmya as fighting on religious principles, while Purohit generalises kṣatriya to soldier. Sankaranarayan makes war itself a duty rather than a good.

32.translation: Happy are the kṣatriyas, Pārtha, who are granted a battle like this, one that arrives unsought as an open door to heaven.
32.nuances: Sukhinaḥ is happy for most, blessed for Purohit, but Sankaranarayan reads it as kṣatriyas desirous of happiness. Purohit personalises the open gate to Arjuna alone and Prabhupada renders heaven as the heavenly planets.

33.translation: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, you will throw away both your duty and your honour and incur sin.
33.nuances: All agree on the three-fold loss; Purohit adds the label traitor, Adidevananda reads kīrti as honoured position, and Prabhupada makes it reputation as a fighter and frames the whole as religious duty.

34.translation: People will also tell of your undying disgrace, and for one who has been honoured, disgrace is worse than death.
34.nuances: There is no disagreement in substance. Bhūtāni is people for five and literally creatures for Sankaranarayan, and sambhāvita is rendered honoured, noble, esteemed or respectable.

35.translation: The great warriors will think you withdrew from the fight out of fear, and those who once held you in high regard will come to think little of you.
35.nuances: Mahārathāḥ is great car-warriors (Sivananda), generals (Purohit, Prabhupada), chariot-riders (Gambirananda), warriors (Adidevananda) or mighty charioteers (Sankaranarayan). Purohit heightens fear to cowardice and despicable, while the others keep the milder lightly held.

36.translation: Your enemies will say many things that should never be said, mocking your ability. What could be more painful than that?
36.nuances: Avācyavādān is abusive words for Sivananda, scandal for Purohit, indecent words for Gambirananda, and words that should never be uttered for Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, with Prabhupada softening to unkind words. Purohit's humiliating replaces the others' painful.

37.translation: If you are killed you will win heaven; if you win you will enjoy the earth. So rise, Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
37.nuances: All six agree on the either-or. Prabhupada again translates svarga as heavenly planets and mahī as earthly kingdom, and Purohit adds kingdom of earth.

38.translation: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, prepare yourself for battle; in this way you will incur no sin.
38.nuances: Sivananda and Prabhupada add the gloss fight for the sake of fighting, which the Sanskrit does not state, while Purohit, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan keep to the plain equanimity instruction. Yujyasva is engage, make ready or gird yourself.

39.translation: This understanding has been set before you from the standpoint of Sāṅkhya; now hear it from the standpoint of Yoga. Joined to this understanding, Pārtha, you will throw off the bondage of action.
39.nuances: Sāṅkhya is left as Sankhya by Sivananda and Adidevananda, glossed as Knowledge by Purohit, Self-realization by Gambirananda and analytical study by Prabhupada, who then reads Yoga as working without fruitive results. Sankaranarayan uniquely reads the same knowledge as serving both Sāṅkhya and Yoga rather than two separate teachings.

40.translation: Here no effort is lost and no harm comes of it; even a little of this practice saves one from great fear.
40.nuances: Pratyavāya is harm for Sivananda and Gambirananda, accrual of evil for Adidevananda, contrary downward course or sin for Sankaranarayan, and repressed for Purohit. Dharma is knowledge or Yoga (Sivananda), Path (Purohit), righteousness (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan) or Dharma called Karma Yoga (Adidevananda).

41.translation: In this path, joy of the Kurus, the resolute understanding is single; the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
41.nuances: Buddhi is determination (Sivananda), intellect (Purohit, Prabhupada), conviction (Gambirananda), mind (Adidevananda) or knowledge (Sankaranarayan). Purohit paraphrases into a statement about steadying the straying intellect and drops the epithet kurunandana.

42.translation: Pārtha, the unwise speak flowery words, delighting in the letter of the Veda and claiming that there is nothing beyond it.
42.nuances: Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan translate verses 42 to 43 or 42 to 44 as a single block, so their renderings cannot be matched line by line. Sivananda and Prabhupada treat the verse alone, Prabhupada adding fruitive activities and heavenly planets; Purohit reads puṣpitā as figurative language rather than flowery.

43.translation: Full of desires and set on heaven, they teach rites laden with specific ceremonies that lead to rebirth as the fruit of action and aim at pleasure and power.
43.nuances: Sivananda and Purohit treat the verse separately, Purohit reading it as people constructing their own heaven; Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan merge it with the surrounding verses. Prabhupada compresses it to a single sentence about sense gratification and opulence.

44.translation: Those who cling to pleasure and power, their minds carried away by such talk, never gain the resolute understanding that is fixed in deep concentration.
44.nuances: Samādhi is kept as Samadhi by Sivananda, read as concentration by Purohit and Sankaranarayan, understood as the mind by Gambirananda and Adidevananda, and rendered by Prabhupada as devotional service to the Supreme Lord. Sankaranarayan's not prescribed for concentration is the most literal handling of na vidhīyate.

45.translation: The Vedas deal with the three guṇas; rise above the three guṇas, Arjuna. Be free from the pairs of opposites, always grounded in sattva, unconcerned with getting and keeping, and possessed of yourself.
45.nuances: Nityasattvastha is read as abiding in the quality of sattva by Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, as steady in truth by Purohit, and as established in the eternal Being by Sankaranarayan, who also reads traiguṇyaviṣaya as the Vedas binding through the Strands. Prabhupada frames guṇas as modes of material nature and yogakṣema as anxieties for gain and safety.

46.translation: As much use as a well has when water floods the land on every side, that much use are all the Vedas to a brāhmaṇa who truly knows.
46.nuances: Most read the simile as devaluing the Vedas for the realised knower, but Purohit inverts it into the skilled theologian taking what serves his purpose, and Prabhupada reads it as the great reservoir serving all purposes of the Vedas for one who knows their purpose. Sankaranarayan turns the brāhmaṇa into an intelligent student of the Vedas.

47.translation: Your entitlement is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not become attached to inaction.
47.nuances: Adhikāra is right for all except Sankaranarayan's claim; karmaphalahetuḥ is motive for Sivananda and Purohit, agent of the results for Gambirananda, cause for Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada. Prabhupada narrows karma to prescribed duty and inaction to not doing your duty.

48.translation: Fixed in Yoga, Dhanañjaya, perform your actions, letting go of attachment and staying the same in success and failure. That evenness is what is called Yoga.
48.nuances: Samatva is evenness of mind (Sivananda, Adidevananda), equanimity (Gambirananda, Prabhupada) or even-mindedness (Sankaranarayan). Purohit reads yogastha as mind concentrated on the Divine and translates Yoga as Spirituality, a theological gloss the others avoid.

49.translation: Mere action falls far short of the Yoga of understanding, Dhanañjaya; seek refuge in understanding. Those driven by the fruits are to be pitied.
49.nuances: Buddhiyoga is Yoga of wisdom for Sivananda and Gambirananda, an intellect concentrated on the Divine for Purohit, evenness of mind for Adidevananda, and devotional service for Prabhupada, who also turns the comparison into keeping abominable activities far distant. Sankaranarayan reads dūreṇa as inferior action staying away at a distance, a quite different construal.

50.translation: One who is joined to understanding sheds both good and bad deeds here in this life. So devote yourself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.
50.nuances: Yoga karmasu kauśalam is skill in action for most, but Purohit reads it as Spirituality is the real art of living and Prabhupada as the art of all work. Sukṛtaduṣkṛte is good and evil deeds, virtue and vice (Gambirananda) or good and bad reactions (Prabhupada).

51.translation: The wise who are joined to understanding give up the fruit born of action; freed from the bondage of birth, they reach the state that is free from all ills.
51.nuances: Padam anāmayam is the place beyond all evil (Sivananda, Gambirananda), highest bliss (Purohit), region beyond all ills (Adidevananda), literally place devoid of illness (Sankaranarayan), and for Prabhupada the state beyond all miseries by going back to Godhead, with devotional service again replacing buddhi.

52.translation: When your understanding has crossed the thicket of delusion, you will grow weary of all that has been heard and all that is still to be heard.
52.nuances: Nirveda is indifference for Sivananda, Purohit and Prabhupada, dispassion for Gambirananda, but disgust for Adidevananda and an attitude of futility for Sankaranarayan. Mohakalila is mire, entanglements, turbidity, tangle, thicket or dense forest.

53.translation: When your understanding, once unsettled by what you have heard, stands still and unshaken in concentration, then you will attain Yoga.
53.nuances: Śrutivipratipannā divides the translators: Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada read it as bewildered or disturbed by Vedic hearing, but Adidevananda reads it as well enlightened by hearing from Me. Samādhi is Self (Sivananda, Gambirananda), contemplation of the Infinite (Purohit), concentration (Sankaranarayan) or trance of self-realization (Prabhupada).

54.translation: Arjuna said: Keśava, how is a person of steady insight, one who stands in deep concentration, to be described? How does such a steady-minded person speak, how sit, how walk?
54.nuances: Bhāṣā is description (Sivananda, Gambirananda), mode of speech (Adidevananda), connotation (Sankaranarayan) or symptoms (Prabhupada). Sankaranarayan uniquely reads the last three verbs as what the term conveys, where he abides and what he reaches, rather than as questions about speaking, sitting and walking.

55.translation: The Blessed Lord said: When a person gives up all the desires that have entered the mind, Pārtha, and is content in the self by the self alone, that person is said to be of steady insight.
55.nuances: Ātmanā is read as the Self by Sivananda, Gambirananda and Prabhupada, as himself by Adidevananda, and as the mind by Sankaranarayan. Prabhupada expands kāmān into desires for sense gratification arising from mental concoction, and Purohit drops the vocative and the technical term sthitaprajña.

56.translation: A sage whose mind is not shaken by sorrows, who has no craving for pleasures, and who is free of passion, fear and anger, is called one of steady mind.
56.nuances: Muni is sage for most but monk for Gambirananda, and Purohit paraphrases sthitadhīḥ as one who stands at that lofty level. Prabhupada inserts the threefold miseries, a technical gloss from his tradition.

57.translation: One who has no fondness for anything anywhere, who neither rejoices nor recoils on meeting good or bad, has an insight that is firmly established.
57.nuances: Anabhisneha is attachment (Sivananda, Gambirananda), love (Adidevananda), desire (Sankaranarayan) or ties of flesh (Purohit). Purohit paraphrases the conclusion as merged in the Infinite and Prabhupada adds in the material world and perfect knowledge.

58.translation: When such a person draws the senses in from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, that person's insight is firmly established.
58.nuances: All six share the tortoise image; Purohit and Prabhupada add the shell. Purohit reads the conclusion as attained Perfection and Prabhupada as perfect consciousness, while the others keep steady wisdom.

59.translation: Sense objects fall away from the embodied one who abstains, but the taste for them remains; even that taste falls away once the Supreme is seen.
59.nuances: Nirāhāra is abstinent for most but literally abstains from food for Sankaranarayan. Param is the Supreme for Sivananda and Sankaranarayan, Truth for Purohit, the Absolute for Gambirananda, the self supreme over the senses for Adidevananda, and a higher taste for Prabhupada.

60.translation: For the turbulent senses, Kaunteya, forcibly carry off the mind even of a discerning person who is striving against them.
60.nuances: The translators agree on the sense; vipaścit is wise (Sivananda, Adidevananda), intelligent (Gambirananda), discerning (Sankaranarayan) or man of discrimination (Prabhupada). Purohit substitutes O Arjuna and leaves vipaścit untranslated.

61.translation: Having restrained them all, one should remain disciplined with me as the highest aim; the insight of one whose senses are under control is firmly established.
61.nuances: Matparaḥ is intent on Me (Sivananda), meditate on Me (Purohit), Me as the supreme (Gambirananda, Adidevananda) or fixes consciousness upon Me (Prabhupada). Sankaranarayan reads yukta as the master of Yoga and āsīta as sit, while Purohit takes it as meditation.

62.translation: When a person dwells on sense objects, attachment to them grows; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger.
62.nuances: Kāma is desire for most, passion for Sankaranarayan and lust for Prabhupada. Gambirananda runs 62 and 63 together but his text is still divisible; otherwise no interpretive split.

63.translation: From anger comes confusion, from confusion the failure of memory, from failure of memory the ruin of understanding, and when understanding is ruined one is lost.
63.nuances: Praṇaśyati is he perishes (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), he is lost (Adidevananda), destruction (Purohit), but Prabhupada reads it as falling down again into the material pool. Buddhināśa is destruction of discrimination, loss of reason, understanding, or capacity to decide.

64.translation: But one whose self is disciplined, who moves among sense objects with senses freed from attraction and aversion and held under the self's control, attains serenity.
64.nuances: Prasāda is peace (Sivananda, Purohit) or serenity (Gambirananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan), but Prabhupada reads it theologically as the complete mercy of the Lord. Purohit adds eternal and Prabhupada adds regulative principles of freedom.

65.translation: In serenity all sorrows come to an end; for the understanding of one whose mind is serene soon becomes steady.
65.nuances: Buddhi is intellect (Sivananda), right discrimination (Purohit), wisdom (Gambirananda), Buddhi untranslated (Adidevananda), capacity to decide (Sankaranarayan) or intelligence (Prabhupada). Prabhupada again inserts threefold miseries and Kṛṣṇa consciousness in brackets.

66.translation: The undisciplined have no understanding, and the undisciplined have no contemplation; without contemplation there is no peace, and for one without peace, where is happiness?
66.nuances: Ayukta is unsteady (Sivananda, Gambirananda), cannot concentrate (Purohit), unintegrated (Adidevananda), not a master of Yoga (Sankaranarayan) or not connected with the Supreme (Prabhupada). Bhāvanā is meditation, concentration or, for Adidevananda, contemplation of the self.

67.translation: For when the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries away one's insight, as the wind carries off a boat on the water.
67.nuances: Most read yat as the mind that follows the senses, but Prabhupada reads it as even one roaming sense carrying away the intelligence. Gambirananda's like the mind diverting a boat appears to be a misprint for wind, and Purohit reverses the image with a tempest tossing a ship.

68.translation: Therefore, mighty-armed one, the insight of one whose senses are wholly withdrawn from their objects is firmly established.
68.nuances: The translators agree on the sense; prajñā pratiṣṭhitā is steady knowledge, established wisdom, firmly set wisdom, stabilized intellect or steady intelligence, and Purohit alone reads it as reason purified.

69.translation: In what is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake; and where beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees.
69.nuances: Five translators keep the night-and-day paradox literally; Purohit paraphrases it as the saint ignoring what the world lives for. Paśyato muneḥ is the sage who sees (Sivananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan), seeing sage (Gambirananda) or introspective sage (Prabhupada).

70.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which stays unmoved though it is filled from every side, so desires enter the one who attains peace, not the one who hankers after desires.
70.nuances: All read the ocean simile alike; the differences are in kāmakāmī, rendered full of desires, carried away by desire, desirous of objects, longing after objects, or striving to satisfy desires. Purohit and Prabhupada speak of rivers where the Sanskrit has only waters.

71.translation: The person who abandons all desires and moves through life without craving, without a sense of mine and without ego, attains peace.
71.nuances: Nirahaṅkāra is egoism (Sivananda), pride (Purohit, Gambirananda), sense of I (Adidevananda), egotism (Sankaranarayan) or false ego (Prabhupada). Sankaranarayan reads carati as consumes objects, a more literal reading than the others' moves about.

72.translation: This is the state of Brahman, Pārtha; having reached it, one is never again deluded. Abiding in it even at the moment of death, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
72.nuances: Brahmanirvāṇa is oneness with Brahman (Sivananda, Purohit), identification with Brahman (Gambirananda), winning the self (Adidevananda), Brahman the Tranquil One (Sankaranarayan), or entering the kingdom of God (Prabhupada), reflecting their Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Gauḍīya leanings. Gambirananda reads antakāle as the closing years of life rather than the moment of death.

73.translation: Oṁ, That is the Real. Thus ends the second chapter, called Sāṅkhya Yoga, in the Upaniṣads of the glorious Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the science of Yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
